design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of the 1992 National Longitudinal Alcohol Epidemiologic Survey (NLAES; 42,862 US adults, the survey analysed for alcohol in grant_1997). Among the 6,447 respondents who had used drugs from any of ten classes nonmedically at least 12 times (lifetime drug use as defined in the paper), the weighted prevalence of lifetime DSM-IV drug abuse without dependence and of lifetime drug dependence, each aggregated across drugs, was tabulated by recalled age at first drug use (13 or younger to 21 or older), overall and by sex and race; logistic regression estimated the change in odds per year of later onset, adjusted for age group, sex, race, family history of alcoholism, duration of drug use and current vs former use.
can_establish: That in a 1992 US household sample of adults who had used a drug nonmedically at least 12 times, those who recalled starting younger more often reported a lifetime DSM-IV drug use disorder (adjusted odds about 4% to 5% lower per year of later onset), and that about 39% of this group had met criteria for drug abuse or dependence at some time.
cannot_establish: Whether early drug use causes later drug use disorders (cross-sectional, recalled onset, no measure of conduct problems, psychopathology or family drug problems); which drug the onset and the disorder concerned (both aggregated across drug classes); or what share of everyone who ever tries a drug develops a disorder (people who used fewer than 12 times were not in the analysis).

sample.recruitment: General-population household sample: NLAES 1992, sponsored by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, fieldwork by the US Bureau of the Census; noninstitutionalized adults aged 18 and older in the contiguous US and the District of Columbia; oversampling of Black and young adult (18–29) respondents; about 92% of selected households and 97% of selected respondents took part (p. 165, Method › Study Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Lifetime drug use was defined as having used drugs in any of ten classes nonmedically at least 12 times (whether per class or in total is not specified): sedatives, tranquilizers, opioids other than heroin, amphetamines, cocaine and crack, cannabis (including THC and hashish), heroin, methadone, hallucinogens, and other drugs such as inhalants and solvents; nonmedical use = without a prescription, in greater amounts, more often or longer than prescribed, or for another reason (pp. 165–166, Drug use, abuse and dependence assessment, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Lifetime drug use in the whole sample (weighted): men 19.5%, women 12.0%, Black 12.3%, nonblack 16.0%, total 15.6% (Table 1, p. 167). Age, education and income of the 6,447 are not reported, nor their numbers by sex and race.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one interview). Missing data are not reported; nor is the number of people at each onset age.
sample.selection_effects: Household survivors only: deaths, institutions and homelessness are outside the frame, which plausibly leaves out some people with early onset and severe disorders. The 12-use threshold selects people beyond experimentation, so the 40% figure in the paper describes them, not everyone who ever tried a drug.

exposure.measurement: Age at first drug use, recalled at the interview. Test-retest kappas for drug-specific onset ages were 0.68 (heroin), 0.69 (sedatives), 0.77 (cocaine) and above 0.92 (tranquilizers, amphetamines, other opioids, cannabis) (p. 166, 4th paragraph). How the overall onset age was derived from the drug-specific questions is not described.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not analysed. Duration of drug use was a covariate but is not defined in this paper.
exposure.polysubstance: Drug classes were aggregated: the drug first used may differ from the drug of the disorder; no drug-specific analysis was done (the authors suggest one, p. 171). Alcohol and tobacco use were not adjusted for; family history of alcoholism was.

comparison.controls: People with later recalled onset of drug use: prevalence tabulated for each year from 13 or younger to 21 or older (Tables 2 and 3, pp. 168–169); regression per year of later onset, with onset entered as a continuous term (pp. 169–170).
comparison.matching: None. Adjusted for age group (18–29 as reference, 30–44, 45–64, 65 and older), sex, race (Black vs nonblack), family history of alcoholism in first-degree relatives, duration of drug use, and current vs former use (p. 167, Statistical Analysis; Table 4, p. 170).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history of drug use disorders was not measured (p. 166); conduct problems, psychopathology, childhood adversity, peers, and age at first drink or first cigarette were not used. Current vs former use may itself follow from the disorder.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS: DSM-IV drug abuse (at least one of four abuse criteria in any one year: continued use despite social or interpersonal problems, recurrent hazardous use, failure to fulfil major role obligations, recurrent drug-related legal problems) and dependence (at least three of seven criteria in any one year), derived for each drug and combined into any drug abuse and any drug dependence; clustering and duration criteria; lifetime = past year or before; the two diagnoses mutually exclusive (abuse = without lifetime dependence) (p. 166, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Test-retest kappas 0.79 (past year) and 0.73 (lifetime) for any drug abuse or dependence (p. 166, 4th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Lifetime DSM-IV drug dependence; lifetime drug abuse among people without lifetime dependence, with abuse criteria that include recurrent drug-related legal problems.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (two outcomes, each also estimated in four subgroups).

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 4 (p. 170): age at onset of drug use, beta −0.05 (SE 0.01; p printed as < .00003) for abuse and −0.04 (SE 0.01; < .01) for dependence. Other coefficients, abuse and dependence: male 0.39 and 0.03 (not significant); Black −0.55 and −0.02 (not significant); family history of alcoholism 0.26 and 0.71; duration of drug use 0.01 and 0.05; former vs current use −0.59 and 0.18; age 30–44 0.02 and −0.51, 45–64 −0.28 and −0.77, 65 and older −0.54 and −4.10 (vs 18–29). Editors' conversion: per-year odds ratios about 0.95 for abuse (approximate 95% CI 0.93–0.97) and 0.96 for dependence (0.94–0.98), that is, 4.9% and 3.9% lower odds per year; the betas are printed to two decimals, so these are rough.
analysis.covariates: Age group, sex, race, family history of alcoholism (first-degree relatives), duration of drug use, current vs former use (p. 167).
analysis.selective_reporting: Subgroup models are reported only as percentage reductions (with 'not significant' for dependence in Black respondents), without estimates or intervals; no unadjusted estimates; model sample sizes not given.
analysis.power: Not reported; 97 to 121 Black respondents with a disorder (unweighted), which the authors suggest may explain the null result in that group (p. 171).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among people who had used a drug at least 12 times, lifetime drug abuse fell from 28.9% (onset at 13 or younger) to 11.1% (21 or older, a total that conflicts with its subgroups) and lifetime dependence from 33.6% to 13.6%, dependence being nearly flat (11% to 15%) for onset at 17 or later. After adjustment, odds were about 5% (abuse) and 4% (dependence) lower per year of later onset. About 20% had lifetime abuse and 19% dependence.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls early onset a significant predictor of the later development of drug abuse and, by a slip, of lifetime alcohol dependence, and gives the per-year reductions as 4% for abuse and 5% for dependence (p. 163); the Results call onset a major contributor to the development of drug abuse and dependence (p. 170); the Discussion calls age at first drug use "a powerful predictor of lifetime drug abuse" in every subgroup and of dependence except in Black respondents (p. 171), and closes by calling early onset a powerful predictor of very serious long-term consequences (p. 172); 40% of all people who use drugs are said to go on to abuse or dependence (pp. 164, 171–172). The authors also ask whether the delay itself or, more likely, a combination of other factors reduces risk, and whether early onset is a modifiable risk factor or a marker (p. 171). Gaps: (1) 'powerful' describes adjusted odds about 4% to 5% lower per year, with dependence flat after 17; (2) the abstract reverses the abuse and dependence figures and names alcohol instead of drug dependence; (3) 'subsequent development' and 'contributor to the development' are causal readings of a cross-sectional association with recalled onset; (4) the 40% applies to people who had used a drug at least 12 times and includes abuse defined partly by legal problems; (5) subgroup statements come without estimates or tests.

timeline.event: Robins and Murphy, young Black men in St Louis: earlier drug use went with greater risk of later problems, as cited by the authors (p. 165).

Robins and Przybeck, St Louis adults aged 18 to 35 with DSM-III criteria: the earlier drug use began, the greater the risk of abuse and dependence, as cited by the authors, who criticize the restricted sample and older criteria (pp. 164–165).

Labouvie, Bates and Pandina: 15-year-old males followed for 13 years; age at onset of drug use did not predict drug-related problems at 30, as cited by the authors, who discount it (men only, a single 3-year window, an aggregate problem measure) (p. 164).
Alcohol counterpart in the same survey: odds of lifetime dependence 14% lower per year of later first drink (read in this round).
This study: NLAES, people who had used a drug at least 12 times; adjusted odds about 5% (abuse) and 4% (dependence) lower per year of later onset.

replication.where_it_stands: The drug counterpart of the alcohol study shows a weaker per-year association, and the only prospective study the authors cite found no prediction (Labouvie et al., 1997). Later prospective and twin tests named on the project's General list (Odgers et al., 2008; Richmond-Rakerd et al., 2016) were not read for this card. Whether early drug use causes later disorders remains open, as the authors acknowledge.

funding.funder: No funding or acknowledgment statement. Both authors were at the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (Division of Biometry and Epidemiology), which sponsored the NLAES (pp. 163, 165).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Government researchers analysing their institute's own survey; no commercial interest is apparent.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that measure conduct problems, family drug problems and other liabilities before any drug use and record use and disorders drug by drug as they happen; comparisons of twins or siblings who differ in age at first use of a particular drug; and long-term follow-up of prevention trials that succeed in delaying first use.

domains.note: Adjusted for age group, sex, race, family history of alcoholism and duration of drug use; family history of drug disorders, conduct problems, psychopathology, childhood adversity and other substance use were not measured or not used; adjustment for current vs former use may itself be affected by the disorder.
Recalled onset; drug-specific reliabilities from 0.68 to above 0.92, but how the overall onset age was derived is not described, and recall may differ between people with and without a disorder.

Household survivors with good response; deaths, institutions and homelessness, plausibly related to both early onset and severe disorder, are outside the frame; the 12-use threshold defines who counts as having used drugs.
Lifetime diagnoses; treatment after onset cannot remove a past diagnosis.
Missing data and the numbers at each onset age are not reported.
Structured lay interview with fair to good reliability (0.73 lifetime); disorders aggregated across drugs and recalled in the same interview as the onset age; abuse partly defined by legal problems.
No unadjusted estimates; subgroup results given as percentages or as not significant, without estimates or intervals; the abstract misreports the main figures.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The gradient in Tables 2 and 3 is a reasonable description of what US adults who had used a drug at least 12 times reported in 1992, from a large probability sample with a standard interview, although one total in Table 2 conflicts with its subgroups. As evidence that early drug use causes drug use disorders it is weak: the exposure was recalled in the same interview as the outcome, the main competing explanations were not measured, the drug first used and the drug of the disorder are not linked, and one covariate may follow from the outcome. Cite it for the cross-sectional association in this group (lifetime dependence 33.6% for onset at 13 or younger against 11% to 15% for onset at 17 or later; adjusted odds about 4% to 5% lower per year) and for the share with abuse (20.1%) or dependence (18.6%) among people who had used a drug at least 12 times; do not cite the abstract's per-year figures (reversed), the 11.1% abuse total for onset at 21 or older (inconsistent with its subgroups), or the paper as showing that delaying first drug use prevents drug use disorders.

key_findings.finding: Lifetime drug use (nonmedical use of drugs in any of ten classes at least 12 times) was reported by 15.6% (SE 0.2) of the weighted NLAES sample: men 19.5%, women 12.0%, Black 12.3%, nonblack 16.0%; 6,447 respondents, about 16% of the sample.
key_findings.locator: Drug use, abuse and dependence assessment, 1st paragraph (starting p. 165); Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (p. 167)

key_findings.finding: Among people with lifetime drug use so defined, 20.1% (SE 0.6) had lifetime drug abuse without dependence (men 22.6%, women 16.3%, Black 13.9%, nonblack 20.7%) and 18.6% (SE 0.6) lifetime drug dependence (men 18.8%, women 18.4%, Black 18.1%, nonblack 18.7%). Editors' sum: 38.7% with either diagnosis, the basis of the paper's statement that 40% of people who use drugs develop abuse or dependence.
key_findings.note: The 40% applies to people who had used a drug at least 12 times, not to everyone who ever tried a drug.

key_findings.finding: Weighted prevalence of lifetime drug abuse without dependence by recalled age at first drug use, total (SE): 13 or younger 28.9% (1.9); 14, 21.5% (2.2); 15, 24.3% (1.9); 16, 25.1% (1.7); 17, 20.3% (1.7); 18, 17.7% (1.5); 19, 18.0% (2.4); 20, 13.6% (2.0); 21 or older 11.1% (0.9). Men had higher prevalence than women at every onset age (for example 30.8% vs 25.5% at 13 or younger; 17.9% vs 6.0% at 20).
key_findings.note: The total for onset at 21 or older (11.1%) is lower than all four subgroup values (11.7% to 13.9%), which is impossible for a weighted total (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Weighted prevalence of lifetime drug dependence by recalled age at first drug use, total (SE): 13 or younger 33.6% (1.9); 14, 26.8% (2.4); 15, 25.4% (1.9); 16, 17.7% (1.3); 17, 15.1% (1.4); 18, 15.0% (1.5); 19, 13.4% (1.9); 20, 11.4% (1.8); 21 or older 13.6% (1.2). Men and women had similar values at most ages (33.8% vs 33.2% at 13 or younger; 13.2% vs 14.1% at 21 or older); in Black respondents prevalence went from 28.9% to 17.8%, irregularly.
key_findings.note: Editors' sums of Tables 2 and 3 (mutually exclusive diagnoses): either disorder 62.5% for onset at 13 or younger, about 35% at 17, about 25% at 20 and at 21 or older.

key_findings.finding: Adjusted for age group, sex, race, family history of alcoholism, duration of drug use and current vs former use, age at onset of drug use had beta −0.05 (SE 0.01) for lifetime abuse and −0.04 (SE 0.01) for lifetime dependence; the authors give these as 5% and 4% lower odds per later year of onset. Family history of alcoholism had beta 0.26 (abuse) and 0.71 (dependence); male sex 0.39 (abuse) but 0.03 (dependence, not significant). Editors' conversion: odds ratios of about 0.95 and 0.96 per year.

By subgroup, the odds of lifetime abuse fell 4% (men), 6% (women), 5% (nonblack) and 2% (Black) per year of later onset, and the odds of dependence 5% (men), 2% (women) and 4% (nonblack); in Black respondents onset was not significantly related to dependence. No estimates, intervals or tests of subgroup differences are given.
key_findings.note: The paragraph says alcohol abuse where drug abuse is meant (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: The authors cite their earlier NLAES report that 76% of onsets of drug use occurred before 19, and a prospective study (Labouvie et al., 1997; males aged 15 followed for 13 years) in which age at onset did not predict drug-related problems at 30, which they discount (men only, one 3-year window, an aggregate measure).

The authors ask whether the delay of drug use itself or, more likely, a combination of other factors reduces the risk of later disorders, whether early onset is a modifiable risk factor or a marker of disorders that would develop anyway, and whether delaying onset could have unintended effects; they call for prospective studies from childhood beyond young adulthood.
Family history of drug use disorders was not measured; family history of alcoholism among first-degree relatives was used as a control instead (kappas 0.65 to 1.00 by type of relative).
key_findings.locator: Drug use, abuse and dependence assessment, 5th and 6th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the per-year reductions as 4% for drug abuse and 5% for dependence, the reverse of Table 4 (beta −0.05 for abuse, −0.04 for dependence), the Results (p. 170) and the Discussion (5% and 4%, p. 171).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite Table 4: about 5% lower odds per year for abuse and about 4% for dependence.

reporting_issues.issue: Several statements name alcohol where drugs are meant: the abstract says early drug use predicted lifetime alcohol dependence (p. 163); the Results speak of the trend in alcohol dependence (p. 169) and of the odds of lifetime alcohol abuse in subgroups (p. 171); and they list duration of drinking among the covariates (p. 169), whereas the Methods and Table 4 say duration of drug use.
reporting_issues.consequence: Wording errors; the tables show that all analyses concern drug use disorders.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 and Figure 1 the total prevalence of abuse for onset at 21 or older (11.1%, SE 0.9) is lower than every subgroup value (men 13.9%, women 11.7%, Black 12.6%, nonblack 13.0%), which is impossible for a weighted total of these groups; the Results repeat the 11.1% (p. 169).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the total or the subgroup values for this onset group are wrong; the end point of the abuse gradient is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The n in the column heads of Tables 2 and 3 are the numbers of people with abuse (1,273) or dependence (1,232), not the denominators, and the Results give n = 1,273 for both abuse and dependence (p. 168); the number of people at each onset age is never given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of each cell can be judged only from its standard error.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 4, the dependence coefficient for age 65 and older (−4.10, SE 1.31) gives p of about .002, not < .0005 as printed; the SE of 0.72 for male sex (dependence) is out of line with the SEs of the other sex, race, family-history and use-status coefficients (0.07 to 0.15) and may be a misprint; several p values cannot be checked because the betas and SEs are printed to two decimals (for example duration of drug use for abuse, 0.01 with SE 0.01, printed p < .043) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the onset coefficients are not affected, but the table is not fully reliable.

reporting_issues.issue: Duration of drug use, a covariate, is not defined, and how the overall age at first drug use was derived from the drug-specific onset questions is not described; whether people with dependence were part of the reference group of the abuse model is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The exposure and a key covariate are not fully specified; if people with dependence were in the abuse model's reference group, the abuse estimate would be diluted.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction describes the 20% with abuse and 19% with dependence as shares of those who have ever used drugs, and the Discussion as shares of all persons who use drugs (pp. 164, 171–172), whereas the Methods count only people who used drugs at least 12 times (p. 166). The Discussion also says abuse was more prevalent in nonblack than Black respondents at each onset age (p. 171), but at onset 14 Table 2 shows 30.3% vs 20.7% the other way (the Results say at most ages, p. 169).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 40% must be cited with the 12-use definition; the race statement should follow the table.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, scanned), pp. 163–173 (all pages; numbers checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi and on Tables 2 to 4 and Figures 1 and 2 rendered at 300 dpi; no supplement)
